description: Every class and method of the scripting API, a line each (also: redgem api).
about: The scripting API of RedGem games: the classes and methods scripts use. Generated from docs/scripting/api.json, which tests keep in step with the engine.
notes: Script errors are logged with a backtrace and only disable the failing behaviour; the game keeps running. Every method takes finite numbers a float can hold: infinity, NaN or a number too large raises an `ArgumentError` instead of reaching the scene. A setting with a range raises outside it and says the range; nothing is quietly clamped, except `Vehicle#drive`'s inputs. Assigning `transform.position` to a physics object teleports it (moving bodies also stop); changing its rotation keeps its velocity. Images may be PNG, JPEG or static WebP (a name without an extension looks for `.webp` last), at most 8192 pixels a side; animated WebP and KTX2/Basis are not read. Missing or unreadable images (scene textures, `UI.image`, particle images) show an opaque magenta-and-black checkerboard, with a warning; a material that never named a texture keeps its plain color, and no path reads outside the game's folder.

classes.notes: `==` compares the numbers exactly, and equal vectors are one key of a `Hash`. A vector used as a key must not be changed in place (`set`, `add!`...) while the `Hash` holds it: use a `dup` as the key. The scene keeps positions, rotations and scales in 32-bit floats, so a vector that goes through it comes back rounded: compare what comes back from the scene with `approx?(other, tolerance)`. The in-place methods change the vector and hand it back: `dup` one you got from someone else first. Arithmetic whose result would not fit a float, and dividing by zero, raise an `ArgumentError`; a vector changed in place is then left as it was.

classes.notes: `layers:` is a layer's name or a list of them (every layer when nil); `ignore:` is an object or a list of objects to see through. Hits are `{object:, point:, normal:, distance:}`, each object once, nearest first, at most 64; triggers are never hit. A cast that starts inside something hits it at distance 0.

classes.about: What holds two bodies together, or one to the world (made by Physics.joint).

methods.name: kind

methods.about: the object it holds

methods.name: other

methods.name: broken?
methods.about: whether it was pulled past its break force

methods.name: remove
methods.about: lets go

methods.name: enabled?
methods.about: whether it holds right now

methods.name: enabled=
methods.about: lets go for a while, or holds again

methods.name: break_force
methods.about: the pull (newtons) or twist (newton meters) it breaks at; 0 never breaks

methods.name: break_force=
methods.about: sets the pull it breaks at

methods.name: motor
methods.about: a hinge turns at that speed (degrees per second) with at most that torque; 0 torque lets it go

methods.name: angle
methods.about: how far a hinge turned from where it started, in degrees

classes.notes: Points and axes are in world space; `anchor:` defaults to the object's position, `other_anchor:` (a distance joint's other end) to the other object's, `axis:` to up. A hinge's `limits:` are degrees [low, high] from where it starts (low -180 to 0, high 0 to 180), a slider's are meters along its axis; a hinge's `motor_speed:` needs a `motor_torque:`. A distance joint keeps between `min:` (0) and `max:` (how far apart the ends are) apart, springy with `spring:` (hertz) and `damping:`. Each kind refuses options it has no use for, and `motor` and `angle` raise for anything but a hinge. A joint needs a dynamic body at one end (one whose bodies were all made kinematic since holds nothing until one is dynamic again); it goes when either object is destroyed or the scene changes.

classes.name: Navigation
classes.about: Where the characters a game moves can walk, and the way from one place to another.

methods.name: path
methods.about: the points to walk through from near `from` to near `to` (Vector3s, both ends included), or nil when there is no way there

methods.name: nearest
methods.about: the walkable point nearest a point (within 8 m of it), or nil

methods.name: walkable?
methods.about: whether a point is on walkable ground, up to a character's height above it

methods.name: draw
methods.about: shows the walkable cells within a radius for this frame, as Debug.box does; returns how many

methods.name: bake
methods.about: bakes the scene's grid again now (a level a script changed); returns what stats does

methods.name: stats
methods.about: how the grid was baked: {columns:, cells:, cell_size:, cells_enlarged:, milliseconds:}

classes.notes: The grid is baked from the scene's static bodies as it loads when game.json has a `navigation` section (`cell_size` 0.25, `agent_radius` 0.4, `agent_height` 1.8, `max_step` 0.4, `max_slope` 45 degrees, `bake_on_load` true), and otherwise when a script first asks. Moving bodies, characters and triggers are not obstacles, and a level changed after the bake is not seen until `Navigation.bake`. A path goes through cells side by side no more than `max_step` apart, never cutting a corner, and is pulled straight. A search looks at no more than 16384 cells: a way longer than that gives nil, as one to a place nobody can reach does. A grid has at most 262144 columns: a larger level is baked with larger cells, with a warning.

classes.notes: Every sound played gets an id, flat (`play`) or positional (`play_at`) alike: `stop`, `playing?` and `set` take either. A sound that does not loop is decoded once and each play is a voice of its own; loops and music stream, so a crossfade plays two tracks for its length. A sound plays in a mix group, `:music`, `:effects` (the default) or `:voice`, and is heard at its volume times the player's volume of its group (`Settings.music_volume`, `effects_volume`, `voice_volume`) times the master volume. A track that cannot play leaves the one playing as it was. `play_at` sources use stereo panning and inverse-distance volume, fading to silence at `max_distance`. `volume` must be 0 or more and `pitch` from 0.01 to 8; `0 < reference_distance < max_distance`. Positions and directions may be arrays or `Vector3`. Update `Audio.listener(position, forward, up)` when the camera moves: nothing follows an object by itself. At most 64 sounds with ids play at once; old ids are never reused.

classes.notes: A focused widget (`focused: true`) is worked by Enter or a gamepad's A, and left and right change it. An anchor (`:top_left`, `:top`, `:top_right`, `:left`, `:center`, `:right`, `:bottom_left`, `:bottom`, `:bottom_right`) makes x and y offsets from that point of the screen, and puts the matching corner of what is drawn there: `UI.text("Lives", anchor: :top_right, x: -20, y: 20)`. With an anchor, a text's box is as wide as `width:` or its widest line, and `align:` lays its lines out inside it; an image is placed by the width and height given. A text breaks at its own line breaks, and with `width:` also at spaces; a word longer than a line is cut between letters. Lines are `UI.line_height(size)` apart (1.25 times the size). Inside `UI.clip`, the pointer outside the box is over nothing drawn in it. The built-in face adds glyphs as they are asked for (Greek, Cyrillic, accented letters, `€`); for another face or script, put a `.ttf` or `.otf` in `fonts/` and set `UI.font`. A missing or unreadable face falls back to the built-in one, with a warning; glyphs a face lacks show as `?`; there is no bidirectional layout or complex-script shaping.

The wheel scrolls it while the pointer is over it, and scrolling away from the focused row stays until the focus moves. `input: false` leaves the keys and the wheel to something else that frame. A bar beside its right edge shows how far it is scrolled.

classes.name: Debug
classes.about: Developer diagnostics: console messages, frame timings and immediate world drawing.

methods.about: says something

methods.about: reports an error

methods.about: starts a fresh profile window when enabled; disabling retains the last summary

methods.about: whether the developer statistics overlay was requested

methods.about: shows frame timings and FPS; showing also enables profiling, hiding leaves collection running

methods.about: a snapshot with samples, fps and latest/mean/peak timings in milliseconds

methods.name: reset_frame_stats
methods.about: clears statistics and discards any unfinished measurement

methods.name: line
methods.about: draws a world-space line for this frame; returns whether it was accepted

methods.name: box
methods.about: draws an axis-aligned wire box with full nonnegative size for this frame; returns whether it was accepted

classes.notes: Profiling is off by default. The overlay uses the shared game HUD, including editor Play and recordings; it is hidden when profiling is off. Timings use the real steady clock, independently of Time.scale or fixed-step replay. The most recent 120 completed frames form the window; reads during a frame expose only completed frames. FPS uses completion-to-completion intervals, and is zero until an interval is available. `latest`, `mean` and `peak` contain `frame_ms`, `interval_ms`, `has_interval`, and `input_ms`, `network_ms`, `http_ms`, `update_ms`, `physics_ms`, `presentation_ms`, `scene_ms`. Input includes pending script startup; network and HTTP include their callbacks; update includes animations, scripts, particles, loading UI and physics. Physics includes fixed-update callbacks, body synchronization and contacts, so its time overlaps update. Presentation includes uploads, drawing and any frame-cap or synchronization waits. Scene includes request polling, synchronous reads and activation; the asynchronous worker is not instrumented, while offline fixed-step waits count as scene wall time. These are foreground wall times, not GPU timers or CPU utilization. Phase times are inclusive and must not be summed as a partition. Overlay timings and captures are nondeterministic; leave the overlay off for reproducible pictures. Debug.line and Debug.box use world coordinates and live for one frame: submit from ready/update/fixed_update. At most 4096 commands are accepted per frame; later calls return false. They are local-only and return false without a presenter, while still validating arguments. depth_test: false draws through objects. Shape frames use unjittered rendering and reset temporal history; normal temporal sampling resumes afterwards. Native windows allocate one cached color/depth target only when shapes are requested; editor, scaled and recorded views reuse their target. If that extra native target is unavailable, the game still draws with a warning and the shapes are omitted.

classes.name: Game
classes.about: The game itself.

methods.name: load_scene
methods.about: switches to scenes/<name>.glb ("main" is scene.glb); Ruby globals survive

methods.name: load_scene_async
methods.about: queues a background scene read; the old world survives failed reads and cancellation

methods.name: loading?
methods.about: a scene request is queued or being read

methods.name: loading_scene
methods.about: the requested scene name, or nil

methods.name: loading_error
methods.about: the last asynchronous read error, or nil; cleared by the next load request

methods.name: cancel_scene_load
methods.about: cancels a pending asynchronous request; returns whether one was pending

methods.name: on_loading
methods.about: draws the loading screen each frame with unscaled delta; no block restores the default

methods.name: scene_name
methods.about: the scene running

methods.name: title
methods.about: the game's title

methods.name: quit
methods.about: ends the game

methods.name: stop_recording
methods.about: ends a video recorded with --record; the game goes on

methods.name: version
methods.about: the version in game.json ("1.2.0"), or nil

classes.notes:
While an asynchronous read is pending, physics, animations and normal behaviour callbacks pause.
Input, networking, HTTP callbacks, audio and presentation continue. The loading callback can use
`UI`, handle cancel buttons and animate using its unscaled delta; `Time.delta` is zero during
loading. The pointer is released while the screen is shown. The default screen draws a translated
loading label over the old world. A callback error is reported once and disables it for that load.

Unsafe names are rejected immediately; missing or unreadable files are reported through
`Game.loading_error` after the request runs. The old world stays intact if reading fails or is cancelled. The most recent request wins;
`Game.load_scene` also supersedes an asynchronous request. Globals survive successful activation,
but the old scene's loading callback is removed before the next scene's setup runs. Errors are
reported through `Game.loading_error` and the event log. At most eight background requests/results can be
outstanding across the process, using one shared reader; a full queue fails without changing the
world. Cancelling an active read discards its result; it does not interrupt the file parser.

Only file reading and glTF parsing happen on the worker. Physics creation, script setup, texture
decoding and GPU upload still happen on the owning thread and may hitch during activation. The
old and incoming scene coexist in memory during reading. Fixed-step offline runs (including
recordings and scripted replays) wait for the reader before advancing, then show exactly one
loading frame before activation so completion does not depend on thread scheduling. Networked runs and dedicated-server rooms keep the
background reader even in fixed-step mode; activation still runs on the server loop and can stall
other rooms sharing that loop. Closing the process waits for an active parser to return.

classes.notes: Values are numbers, texts, true/false, `Vector3`, and arrays and hashes of those; hashes come back with string keys. Named slots start on default for every engine and keep their selection across scenes. Selection is local to each engine, including shared-database server rooms. Names are 1–48 lowercase ASCII letters/digits, hyphens or underscores, starting with a letter/digit. At most 64 named stores may be opened per run/local backend and 4096 names listed; invalid names or unavailable backends leave selection unchanged and raise a Ruby error. The existing default file/table is preserved. Named files use their own atomic writes/backups; SQLite uses separate slot tables. Save.update writes to its entry store even if its block selects another slot. Slots keep values, not object-state snapshots or migration metadata.
